label: The Need for Control
framing: The need to control is fear wearing the mask of responsibility. Underneath the spreadsheets and the clenched plans is a quiet belief that if you ever loosen your grip the whole thing falls, and Scripture answers it not by promising you will keep control but by telling you who actually holds it.
cultural: We are trained to believe that with enough planning, enough information, enough effort, we can secure our lives against loss. It is a powerful lie, and it makes the controlling person exhausting to live near and exhausting to be. The illusion breaks the moment a diagnosis or a death or a child's free will reminds us how little was ever in our hands.
historical: The rich fool of Jesus' parable built bigger barns to secure his future and died the same night. The letter of James, written to scattered believers in the first century, mocked the merchant who said today or tomorrow we will go and trade and make a profit, when he did not know what tomorrow would bring. The wisdom tradition had said it long before, that a man plans his way but the Lord directs his steps.
application: Name the fear that your control is managing, since you cannot surrender what you will not see. Practice deliberate handing-over, in prayer and in act, releasing what was never yours to hold. Plan, work, and prepare, for that is faithful, but hold the plan with an open hand and add, if the Lord wills. And let the people you love make their own choices, which is the hardest letting-go of all.

verses.text: A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.
verses.where: A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps. The site's note says the chapter opens with the densest group of sayings about the LORD in the whole collection: people make plans, weigh their motives and cast lots, but the LORD weighs hearts, establishes steps and decides outcomes. Planning is assumed; deciding outcomes is not ours.

verses.text: Many plans are in a man’s heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail.
verses.where: Many plans are in a man's heart, the proverb says, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail. The site's note on the chapter sets the plans of the human heart beside the purpose of the LORD that stands. A person can hold many plans and still rest, because the outcome that matters most is held by someone else.

verses.text: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.” You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.”
verses.where: James rebukes those who plan their business as if tomorrow were theirs to command: you do not even know what will happen tomorrow, he says, and your life is a mist. The site's note puts it that way. He does not forbid planning; he tells them to say if the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.

verses.text: Now Abram’s wife Sarai had borne him no children, but she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar. So Sarai said to Abram, “Look now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Please go to my maidservant; perhaps I can build a family by her.” And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
verses.where: After ten years without the child God promised, Sarai gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram so that she might build a family through her. The site's note says Sarai names the LORD as the reason she needs the plan, Abram agrees without a word, and neither asks God. The plain note says her pain was real, that it did not excuse what followed, and that the person who paid for the plan was Hagar. Grasping at God's promise by our own means usually costs someone else.

verses.text: Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you. Go out to the flock and bring me two choice young goats, so that I can make them into a tasty dish for your father—the kind he loves. Then take it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies.”
verses.where: When Rebekah overhears Isaac planning to bless Esau, she gives Jacob his orders: two young goats, the dish Isaac loves, and the blessing taken by disguise. The site's note says she plans every step, and Jacob's part is to obey. The deception works, and it ends with Esau vowing to kill his brother and Jacob fleeing. Control can win the moment and wreck the family.

verses.text: “What have you done?” Samuel asked. And Saul replied, “When I saw that the troops were deserting me, and that you did not come at the appointed time and the Philistines were gathering at Michmash, I thought, ‘Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.’ So I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering.” “You have acted foolishly,” Samuel declared. “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you; if you had, the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time.
verses.where: Waiting for Samuel at Gilgal while his frightened troops scatter, Saul offers the burnt offering himself. When Samuel arrives just as he finishes, Saul explains that he felt compelled. The site's note says Samuel then announces that Saul's kingdom will not endure. Fear of what will happen if we wait is one of the oldest reasons for seizing control.

verses.text: “Be still and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth.”
verses.where: The psalm ends with God's own voice: be still and know that I am God. The site's plain note says be still is not first about feeling calm but about letting go of control: the plans, the worry, the fight you think you must win alone. It asks what you are gripping that God is asking you to drop.

verses.text: Since no one knows what will happen, who can tell him what is to come? As no man has power over the wind to contain it, so no one has authority over his day of death. As no one can be discharged in wartime, so wickedness will not release those who practice it.
verses.where: The Teacher observes that no one knows what will happen, and that no one has power over the wind to contain it, or authority over the day of his death. The site's note says he concludes that no one, however wise, can comprehend the work of God. There are things no amount of effort will put in our hands.

verses.text: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, or marked off the heavens with the span of his hand? Who has held the dust of the earth in a basket, or weighed the mountains on a scale and the hills with a balance? Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor? Whom did He consult to enlighten Him, and who taught Him the paths of justice? Who imparted knowledge to Him and showed Him the way of understanding?
verses.where: Isaiah asks who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and who has directed the Spirit of the LORD or served as his counselor. The site's note says the questions confront the exiles' despair with the size of God, who needs no counselor. A person who has to manage everything has, in a sense, appointed themselves God's advisor.

verses.text: Jesus replied, “You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.”
verses.where: When Jesus comes to wash Peter's feet, Peter recoils, and Jesus answers that he does not realize now what Jesus is doing, but later he will understand. The site's plain note says Peter found it harder to be served than to serve, as many people do, and asks whether we can let Jesus do for us what we cannot do for ourselves. Letting go of control sometimes means letting ourselves be helped.

links.label: Practical guides for the inner life

misread.taken: The parable of the rich fool and his barns is sometimes taken to mean that saving and planning are themselves a lack of trust, so that a careful person is told their prudence is sin, or a controlling person decides that planning less will cure them.
misread.says: The site's plain note says the story is not against saving money or planning for the future: Scripture praises Joseph and the ant for storing up. The rich man's sin is what the story names, greed and storing up treasure for himself while not being rich toward God; he planned a life with no one else in it and thought his life was secured by what he owned. Plans are not the problem. Trusting them to hold a life together is.
misread.text: Then he said, ‘This is what I will do: I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones, and there I will store up all my grain and my goods. Then I will say to myself, “You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry!”’

whole: The need for control rarely calls itself that. It calls itself being responsible, being prepared, having high standards, or simply caring. It shows up as the parent who must know where everyone is every hour, the colleague who redoes other people's work, the spouse who manages the calendar, the money and the moods, the person who cannot relax until every possible problem has been planned for. Underneath there is usually fear: that if I loosen my grip, something will fall apart, someone will be hurt, or I will be exposed. It is exhausting for the one who carries it and often for everyone around them. If control has turned into controlling another person, checking their phone, limiting their friends, deciding their choices, that is a harm to be faced honestly; and if someone is controlling you, your safety comes first, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Scripture shows the need for control in some of its most familiar families. Sarai, after years of waiting, took God's promise into her own hands, and Hagar paid for it. Rebekah planned every step of Jacob's deception, and it won the blessing and broke the family. Saul could not bear to wait for Samuel while his army scattered, and offered the sacrifice himself. Each of them had a real fear and a real reason. Each of them decided that God's timing or God's way could not be trusted to work, and acted as if everything depended on them. James puts the deeper problem plainly: we talk about tomorrow as if it were ours to command. Most of us have done the same, and it usually begins as love.

So the Bible's wisdom is to plan, and then to hold the plans in an open hand. Make the plan, and say if the Lord is willing. Do your part faithfully, and leave the outcome to the one who determines the steps. Notice where control is costing someone else, as Sarai's cost Hagar, and stop. Practice small acts of letting go: let someone else do a task their way, leave a question unanswered for a day, receive help without managing it, as Peter had to let Jesus wash his feet. Be still, the psalm says, and know who is God; the stillness is not only a feeling but a decision to stop the fight you think you must win alone. A pastor or a counselor can help where the fear runs deep.

The hope Scripture gives is that the world is not resting on your shoulders, because it rests on God's. He measures the waters in the hollow of his hand, needs no counselor, and his purpose will prevail. The same Jesus who knew where he came from and where he was going knelt with a towel. To let go of control is not to stop caring. It is to trust that the one who holds all things is better at holding them than we are, and that he holds us too.
deep.sit: What are you gripping most tightly right now, and what do you fear would happen if you loosened your hold on it?

prayer.lead: A prayer of a soul learning to rest in God alone. The site's plain note says rest here is not doing nothing; it is stopping the inner struggle and trusting God with it, and the psalmist has to tell his own soul to do it.
prayer.text: In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him. He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken.

careLines.text: The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
